findings.title: Different names, one addressee
findings.claim: The alternatives Allah and al-Rahman widen the qualities through which the addressee is approached while the singular possession gathers the names under one referent. The wider name passages make that plurality usable in invocation without partitioning the one being addressed.
findings.mechanism: The repeated calling forms keep the act of invocation constant as its named object changes from Allah to al-Rahman; the following plural al-asma al-husna is gathered by singular lahu. In 7:180 the beautiful names are joined to calling Him by them, while 20:8 and 59:24 place the same names with a singular divine referent. The paired Rahman and Rahim in 1:3 makes mercy a quality-bearing designation, and 72:18 supplies a boundary against invoking another alongside Allah.
findings.reader_payoff: Name plurality becomes a range of approaches and qualities addressed to one recipient, rather than a multiplication of divine centers.
findings.containment: The names need not be interchangeable for their plurality to converge on one referent. The focus does not establish an etymology for every name; its singular possessor carries the convergence. The reader-supplied cues about 17:108-109 and 17:111 remain attributed because their target surfaces are not present in this packet.

epistemic.reason: A trusted cross-run finding supplies exact focus anchors and the cited connections supply target Arabic, but target morphology is absent. The represented reader-walk contexts are legacy-unbound and are retained only as attributed cues.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: The several designations function as distinct approaches to one called referent.
branch_activations.boundary: This does not make the names semantically identical or infer that every name has the same quality.

findings.title: Prayer as a sought acoustic route
findings.claim: Prayer voice is framed as a route actively sought between raised exposure and a sound that can approach disappearance. Wider address scenes place public and hidden calling in distinct settings, while the attributed preceding recitation sequence lets the route be heard as deliberate pacing and reception rather than a fixed volume point.
findings.mechanism: The focus places tajhar and tukhafit under parallel prohibitions, then uses an effortful seek verb with bayna and sabil. The high and low poles meet in a path that connects them and must be sought. Outside the focus, 71:8 gives an openly voiced call, 7:55 and 7:205 give restrained or inward address, and 20:7 places loud speech beside what is secret and more hidden. The legacy wide reader attributes pacing and embodied reception to 17:106-109; this cue is carried as attributed context.
findings.reader_payoff: The middle becomes an active practice of keeping prayer audible without turning it into public performance or letting it disappear. It is a route to seek in context, not a single universal volume setting.
findings.containment: The cited public and hidden invocations occur in their own settings and do not prescribe one register for every act. The 17:106-109 connection is legacy-attributed, and the supplied context has no target morphology. The fading branch is bounded at the edge of audibility: the focus does not say that prayer becomes silent or that sound literally dies.

epistemic.reason: The trusted cross-run finding anchors the focus voice, interval, and path branches. Exact Arabic is supplied for wider connection targets, but their morphology is not; represented reader-walk evidence for privacy and the 17:106-109 sequence is legacy-unbound and remains attributed.

findings.title: Names as signs of qualities
findings.claim: The focus's names can be heard as more than address labels: al-Rahman and al-husna let a designation point toward a quality, while a wider naming scene presents names as teachable identifiers. The physical-sign branch supplies only an exploratory analogy for that knowledge-bearing force.
findings.mechanism: Al-asma is the carrier; al-Rahman and al-husna are distinct quality-bearing triggers within the focus. In 2:31, names are taught and then requested for the things presented, supplying an independent scene in which names enable identification. Their contact makes it possible to hear a name as indicating something about its referent.
findings.reader_payoff: A name may disclose a quality of its referent as well as make that referent addressable.
findings.containment: The analogy is limited: 2:31 supports names as teachable identifiers, not physical brands or a claim that every name exhaustively reveals divine character. The focus's ordinary naming and invocation remain intact.

epistemic.reason: The focus root option, its independent quality-bearing names, and the exact Arabic supplied for 2:31 create a possible sign-to-quality relation. Target morphology is absent, and the move from physical indication to verbal designation is analogical.

branch_activations.resulting_reading: The names may disclose something about their referents instead of functioning only as call labels.
branch_activations.boundary: The focus does not describe a literal visible mark; the transfer from bodily indication to verbal naming remains analogical.

findings.title: The named addressee and the lowered voice
findings.claim: A wider address scene places the caller, al-Rahman, and voices reduced to a whisper together. Returning to 17:110, the same named addressee and the instruction to seek a prayer-voice path become connected parts of address: who is called and how sound is carried meet, while the focus keeps both loudness and muffling in view.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies calling forms, the name al-Rahman, and the two prayer-voice limits. In 20:108, following the caller leads to voices humbled toward al-Rahman until only whispering is heard. That independent scene returns through the focus's call, name, and low-voice word, tying naming and vocal delivery into one wider relation.
findings.reader_payoff: The transition from divine names to prayer volume becomes a relation between the addressee and the manner of address, rather than two unrelated instructions.
findings.containment: 20:108 is an eschatological scene, not the same prayer act. Its whisper does not set the focus's target volume or cancel the command to seek a path between raised and lowered speech.

epistemic.reason: The connection supplies exact target Arabic and a direct phrase-level contact, but target morphology and an independent trust label are not supplied; the scene difference remains material.
